stories.title: Google's Worst Day Ever Was Made by Its Own AI
stories.story:
For two decades, Google Search was the closest thing capitalism had to a toll road: nearly everyone used it, nearly every advertiser paid for it, and the money flowed without meaningful friction. That era may be ending — and Google's own decisions are partly responsible.

On October 29, Alphabet shed nearly $500 billion in market value in a single session, its worst day since going public in 2004 and the second-largest single-day market-cap loss in U.S. history, behind only Nvidia's DeepSeek shock in January 2025. The trigger was a Q3 earnings report that disappointed on almost every line. Search revenue grew just 12% year-over-year, decelerating sharply from 17% in Q2 and 19% in Q1. Earnings per share came in at $2.12 against analyst models of $3.02. Alphabet also reported negative free cash flow of roughly $9 billion as it pours capital into data centers and AI models.

The structural problem is almost elegant in its irony. Google built AI Mode — its answer to ChatGPT — directly into Search, and users are adopting it. But AI Mode monetizes at lower rates than the classic ten-blue-links format it replaces. Google is cannibalizing its own ad engine while simultaneously funding the cannibalization with record capital expenditure. Competitors like OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude are pulling queries away from Google altogether, and Reddit reported losing over a million weekly Google referrals during October alone, suggesting the top of the funnel is shrinking industry-wide.

The implication is larger than one bad quarter. Wall Street has been willing to fund the AI spending spree on the assumption that core businesses would stay profitable. Google just showed that assumption has a crack in it — and investors now have to wonder whether the same crack runs through every hyperscaler report that follows.
stories.hook: Google didn't lose half a trillion dollars to a competitor — it lost it to a version of itself it can't yet charge for.

stories.title: The $6.3 Billion Hack That Rewrote Ethereum's Safety Assumptions
stories.story:
On the evening of October 29, a single transaction drained approximately $6.36 billion from Binance's hot wallets across ten blockchains — the largest theft in the history of crypto, surpassing every prior record. The mechanism was elegant in its simplicity and devastating in its implications.

The weapon was EIP-7702, a feature introduced in Ethereum's Pectra upgrade that allows a standard wallet to temporarily hand its behavior over to a smart contract. In principle, it enables powerful new account features. In practice, it gave an attacker a skeleton key. After apparently compromising a DevOps engineer's laptop, the attacker used a leaked signing credential to prepare 50 EIP-7702 authorization requests in a single bundled transaction — a "nonce spray" designed to ensure one would land on the correct wallet state. One did. Within four minutes, Binance Hot Wallet 14 was converted into a sweeper contract, forwarding every incoming asset to an address the attacker controlled.

Binance confirmed the breach within hours and pledged to cover all customer losses. By October 30, coordinated action by Tether, Circle, and Ripple had frozen roughly $2.7 billion of the stolen funds. TRM Labs attributed the attack with high confidence to North Korea's TraderTraitor group, the same operation behind the earlier Bybit hack.

The deeper issue is structural. EIP-7702 was celebrated as a step toward smarter, more flexible wallets. The Binance attack demonstrates that any feature expanding what a wallet can authorize also expands the surface that a compromised key can destroy. The theft didn't exploit a bug — it exploited a feature working exactly as designed. Security firms that flagged the suspicious Type-4 delegation transaction in real time were not integrated into Binance's withdrawal pipeline. That gap, between detection and action, is where $6.3 billion disappeared.
stories.hook: The hack didn't exploit a flaw in Ethereum — it exploited a feature that worked perfectly.

stories.title: Intel Beat the Quarter and Collapsed Anyway
stories.story:
Intel did everything Wall Street asked. In Q3 2026, it reported adjusted earnings of $0.52 a share against a consensus of $0.40, and revenue of $16.5 billion — a 21% jump from a year earlier. Its data center and AI division surged 78%. By any backward-looking measure, the turnaround under CEO Lip-Bu Tan was working.

Then came the guidance. For Q4, Intel projected revenue of $15 to $16 billion and adjusted EPS of just $0.25. Analysts had penciled in $17 billion and $0.43. The stock fell more than 22% in after-hours trading — erasing roughly $50 billion in market value on a night the company technically beat expectations.

The mechanism behind the collapse is a collision of two separate crises arriving at once. On the consumer side, global PC shipments fell 4% in Q2 alone, and Intel now forecasts a further 12% contraction in PC demand in 2026, followed by a 10% drop in 2027. Its client computing division — still its largest business — fell 5% year-over-year to $8.1 billion. On the enterprise side, a factory shutdown in Israel caused a $300 million hit and created supply constraints that capped what would otherwise have been a breakout quarter for the data center unit.

The irony is sharp. Intel spent two years restructuring to reposition itself for the AI hardware boom, and the AI orders are genuinely arriving — but its foundry can't fill them fast enough, while the legacy PC business it depends on for cash flow is shrinking faster than the AI business can compensate. The market read the guidance not as a bump but as a structural trap: a company caught between an old revenue base that is deflating and a new one that is supply-constrained. What the earnings season revealed across the hyperscalers is that AI demand is real and vast. What Intel revealed is that being a supplier to that demand is harder than being its customer.
stories.hook: Intel proved you can beat the quarter and still lose the argument.
stories.source: CNBC, Quartz, Investing.com — Intel Q3 2026 earnings coverage

stories.title: Amazon Is Spending $220 Billion to Stay Ahead of Itself
stories.story:
Amazon reported third-quarter results Thursday that were, by almost any conventional measure, extraordinary: AWS grew 39% year-over-year to $46 billion in quarterly revenue, its fastest pace in nearly five years, and operating income surged 61%. Yet the stock fell more than 6% in after-hours trading. The paradox is instructive.

The market was not punishing Amazon for what AWS produced. It was punishing Amazon for what AWS now consumes. Capital expenditures hit $75.9 billion in the quarter alone — more than double the $35.1 billion spent in the same period a year earlier, and well above the $58.7 billion analysts had modeled. For the full year, the company is holding its guidance at roughly $220 billion, almost all of it directed at data centers and AI chips. That spending flipped Amazon's free cash flow to a negative $42.4 billion for the quarter, a hole that would swallow most Fortune 500 companies whole.

CEO Andy Jassy's message was simple and unsettling in equal measure: even at $220 billion, Amazon cannot build fast enough to satisfy demand. He projected AWS growth exceeding 40% in both 2027 and 2028, and said spending next year will be "meaningfully more." The arithmetic of that promise is what investors are sitting with. AWS is already a $184 billion annualized revenue run rate business. To keep growing it at 40%, Amazon must essentially add another mid-sized cloud company every year — in hardware, power, and people — before that capacity can earn a dollar.

What this reveals is a structural shift in how the AI infrastructure race is financed. It is no longer funded by profit; it is funded by the credibility of future profit. Amazon is effectively issuing a multi-hundred-billion-dollar bet that the demand it cannot yet fulfill will eventually pay for the infrastructure it is building to fill it.
stories.hook: Amazon's cloud is growing faster than almost any business its size ever has — and that's exactly why the stock is falling.

stories.title: The Fed Just Quietly Gave Itself Fewer Chances to Act
stories.story:
On October 28, two days before today, the Federal Reserve did something it has not done in roughly four decades of modern central banking: it restructured its own decision-making calendar. Chairman Kevin Warsh, holding rates steady at 3.75–4.00%, announced that starting in 2027 one of the Fed's eight annual meetings will be converted to a strategy-only session — no rate vote, no policy statement. By 2028, two meetings will carry that designation, leaving the FOMC with just six formal rate decisions per year.

The timing is striking. Inflation is running at 3.7%, two dissenting members wanted an immediate hike, and futures markets are already pricing in a December increase followed by more in 2027. In other words, Warsh is trimming the number of decision points precisely when the economy may demand more intervention, not less. His stated rationale is philosophical: the Fed needs space for long-term strategic thinking — on its balance sheet, on inflation frameworks, on productivity — not just an endless cycle of hold-or-hike verdicts.

But the structural consequence cuts against that calm. Fewer formal meetings means each remaining one carries more weight. Markets will front-run those six dates more aggressively. Volatility windows will concentrate. The Fed's traditional escape valve — acting at an unscheduled meeting in a crisis — becomes more loaded symbolically when the bar for convening has been effectively raised by design. Warsh has also explicitly rejected forward guidance, meaning markets get less information at fewer scheduled moments.

What Warsh is really doing is remaking the Fed in his own image: less chatty, more deliberate, less beholden to the eight-times-a-year drumbeat that has shaped market psychology since 1981. Whether that discipline holds when inflation proves stubborn or a shock arrives is the test no calendar reform can schedule.
stories.hook: The Fed just decided it needs fewer meetings — right when the economy might need more answers.
stories.source: CNBC, Yahoo Finance, Global Finance Magazine — October 28–30, 2026
